title: Preventing Sourdough Focaccia from Sticking to Steel Pans
meta_description: Stop your sourdough focaccia from sticking to steel pans. Learn the best oiling techniques and why silicone baking mats are a game-changer for easy release.
html:
There is nothing more heartbreaking than spending three days nurturing a sourdough starter and patiently proofing a high-hydration dough, only to have the bottom half of your masterpiece fuse to your baking pan. Sourdough focaccia is notoriously sticky because of its high water content and the way wild yeast interacts with metal surfaces.

If you are struggling to find the perfect sourdough focaccia non stick pan setup, you aren't alone. Most of us use standard steel baking sheets or cake pans, which are great for heat conduction but terrible for release if you don't have a strategy. Here is how to ensure your bread slides right out every single time.

The Role of Fat in Non-Stick Success

When it comes to sourdough, a light spray of oil isn't enough. You need a significant barrier between the dough and the steel. I recommend using extra virgin olive oil—not just for the flavor, but because it creates a fried crust that naturally separates from the pan.

Pour a generous amount of olive oil into the bottom of your pan and use your fingers or a pastry brush to coat the corners and sides. When you transfer your dough into the pan, dimple it right into that oil. The oil should seep into those craters, creating a protective layer that prevents the gluten from bonding to the metal.

Why Steel Pans Struggle with Sourdough

Steel pans, especially those that have lost their factory seasoning or have small scratches, create microscopic anchors for sourdough. As the bread bakes and the moisture evaporates, the dough can essentially "glue" itself to these imperfections. This is why many bakers hunt for a dedicated sourdough focaccia non stick pan, but the truth is that the accessory you put inside the pan matters more than the pan itself.

If you find that your bread sticks despite heavy oiling, your pan might be too thin, causing the bottom to sear and stick before the internal structure of the bread has set.

The Ultimate Hack: Silicone Baking Mats

If you are tired of the "hope and pray" method of oiling your steel pans, it is time to switch to a physical barrier. I highly recommend using Silicone Baking Mats. These non-stick, reusable mats replace parchment paper and provide a consistent, slick surface that sourdough simply cannot cling to.

Unlike parchment, which can sometimes ripple or tear under a heavy, oily focaccia dough, Silicone Baking Mats lay flat and distribute heat evenly. This ensures that the bottom of your focaccia gets an even, golden-brown crisp without the risk of sticking. Plus, the zero-scrub cleanup means you aren't spending twenty minutes scrubbing burnt olive oil and dough remnants out of your steel pan.

Step-by-Step Guide for a Clean Release

To get the best results regardless of your equipment, follow this sequence:

  • Prep the surface: Line your steel pan with Silicone Baking Mats or apply a heavy layer of olive oil.
  • The Second Proof: Let the dough proof in the pan for at least 2-4 hours. This allows the dough to relax and settle into the oil/mat.
  • The Dimple: Use your fingertips to press deep holes into the dough, pushing it firmly against the non-stick surface.
  • The Post-Bake Rest: Once you pull the pan from the oven, let the focaccia sit for 5-10 minutes. This allows the steam to redistribute, which often helps the bread release more easily.
  • The Lift: Use a thin metal spatula or a bench scraper to gently lift the edges before sliding the whole loaf onto a cooling rack.

Comparing Parchment vs. Silicone for Focaccia

Many bakers use parchment paper as a quick fix for a sourdough focaccia non stick pan experience. While parchment works, it has a few drawbacks. First, it's single-use, creating waste. Second, parchment can sometimes absorb too much oil, leaving the bottom of the bread slightly dry in spots.

Silicone Baking Mats are a superior alternative because they are reusable and create a more uniform heat transfer across the bottom of the steel pan. This leads to that coveted "fried" bottom texture that defines a great focaccia, while ensuring the bread slides off the mat with zero resistance.

FAQ

Can I use butter instead of olive oil?

You can, but it's not recommended. Butter has a lower smoke point than olive oil and contains milk solids that can actually burn and stick to the pan at the high temperatures required for focaccia.

Why does my focaccia stick even when I use a non-stick spray?

Non-stick sprays are often too thin for high-hydration sourdough. They evaporate quickly in the oven, leaving the dough to make direct contact with the pan. A thick layer of oil or a silicone mat is far more effective.

Do I need to grease my Silicone Baking Mats?

While the mats are naturally non-stick, I still recommend a drizzle of olive oil on top of the mat. This isn't to prevent sticking, but to ensure your focaccia has that signature golden, crispy bottom crust.
